speechtext: And Dutchmen's breeches.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
If a responsible leader of a responsible party thinks it well to argue along such lines, I hesitate to say what effect his other arguments will have upon the ordinary men of the street or upon the ordinary members who sit on the back benches of this side of the house. For me it certainly discounts much of his other reasoning.

Marketing Act-Mr. Bury
May I turn for a minute, in the time that is left to me, to the speeches of the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) and the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Moore). When I listened to the hon. member for Weyburn I could not help thinking of two works of English literature. There was an Englishman who lived at the end of the seventeenth and the beginning of the eighteenth century named Edward Young, I have no doubt an ancestor of my hon. friend. He is known to posterity and literature as the author of a very voluminous work, I think in nine volumes; I never had the courage to read them because I have nightmares enough naturally without adding to them artificially. His work is entitled Night Thoughts. The second work that was brought to my recollection in hearing the hon. gentleman's speech was a very exquisite little lyric of two verses written by an Englishman who died in 1921 and who therefore was a man of just yesterday, F. W. Bourdillon, whose lines are known to nearly everyone in the house:
The night has a thousand eyes,
The day but one.
The second verse commences:
The mind has a thousand eyes,
The heart but one.
And the moral of the verses is that the thousand eys are no good and the only eye that is good to give light either in physical or in moral or mental matters is in the one case the one eye of the day, and in the other the single eye of the heart. It seemed to me, as the hon. gentleman was speaking, that in order to damn a bill with whose principle he absolutely disagreed, instead of addressing himself to the principle, he went back to his ancestor and to Bourdillon and borrowed the thousand eyes of his ancestor's night to scrutinize meticulously and microscopically every clause and subclause, every phrase and word which might by any conceivable method of misrepresentation or twisting be made liable to abuse. Then he heaped all those words and phrases, clauses and subclauses, with their gigantic and innumerable possibilities of abuse on the floor in the centre of the chamber and asked: How can you gentlemen pass a bill that is liable to such enormous and multitudinous abuses? Now I should like to say a word or two with regard to the very moving and weighty speech of the hon. member for Ontario. The hon. gentleman is an avowed apostle of laissez-faire; you might sum up all that he had to say by way of argument on this bill in two words: "Hands off." Don't interfere with the principle of free production and free marketing by the individual. The work of production and of marketing are the twin arks of the cult of industry and trade, and the impious hands of no government, nor of any board created by a government, must be allowed to be stretched out to touch them for the purpose of steadying them, however much the carts on which they go may threaten to overturn. But a hundred pairs of other hands, thrust forward from every direction over the whole of this dominion, animated by any and every motive that may be conceived and, working for any different end, may push and jostle, shake and rock those arks to imminent disaster, and yet nothing will happen. Why? Because nature, as she has laws in the physical world, has laws in the economic world also, and nature will so operate through her economic laws, under and through, over and upon these two hundred hands working from different directions and for different ends, as to resolve all their conflicting forces into one resultant which will establish steadiness and progress.
That is a wonderful picture, Mr. Speaker, but is it anything else? Have we not known in the history of Canadian trade and of the trade of other countries that this theory will not work? Have not other countries awakened to that fact and determined to put into operation the principle which is embodied in this bill? Are we not to-day facing the competition of those other countries? What will be the fate of our trade unless we are prepared to adopt the part of wisdom and regulate our exports?
Let me take another line. I am not now concerned with the producers; I am con-concerned only with the great mass of humanity in Canada whose welfare depends upon the trade of this country. Burke has a wonderful phrase, true in part and false in the remainder. He speaks about a great body of people "who have been doomed by providence to live upon trust." I deny the "doom" as I deny the "providence;" but I admit the "trust." I cannot think of a more tragic condition than that great numbers of the people

of this country, for the last four years and more, have been compelled to live so terribly upon trust. Most of us here do not have to live upon trust; we have something more substantial at our backs. That is what we need1; we must have improvement in our trade. We cannot play fast and loose with the trade of Canada, and if that trade is suffering by reason of uncontrolled marketing in foreign markets and in Great Britain, the only great market we have to-day, then I say it is the duty of this house and of this country to support any measure that will bring back trade and that will enable us, in competition with the regulated trade of other countries, to secure that which we have been given a chance of securing and keeping through those gTeat imperial agreements which were obtained by this government two years ago.

The moment any body of producers comes to a government and says, "We are a key industry of this country, and the well-being of the country depends upon our 'being able to carry on our business successfully," whether they be wheat producers, coal producers or any other body oi producers, at that moment is created the right of the government and of the people of the country, the taxpayers whose money must be used for this purpose, to say, " We have the right to know that your business is being carried on efficiently and economically, and that our money will not ibe thrown down a sink hole." That is an absolute correlative right enuring to any government as the result of any form of assistance, whether it be by means of subsidies, lower freight rates made possible only by government payments or anything else; it is the right of the taxpayer who supplies the money to see that the business of the producers and exporters is carried on as effectively and economically as possible.

Mr. Speaker, the preamble of this bill No. 51, under consideration reads as follows:
An act to improve the methods and practices involved in the marketing of natural products in Canada and in export trade, and to make further provision in connection therewith.
I see in this bill a total upheaval of trade in Canada. Up to the present, our Canadian trade was highly organized. We have in London, a High Commissioner, in other countries, like France, Japan and the United States, legations; in every country trade commissioners ; provinces have even their own trade agents in all European countries. The provinces of our Confederation have burdened their budget in order to send to these countries of Europe and even Asia, representatives, experts in trade, who keep in close touch with the provinces in order to market most advantageously the products of this country. The department of Agriculture was in the best of shape when he left office in 1930. Heads of industries also did their utmost to carry on trade relations so as to sell their products on the markets of the Empire and Europe. To-day, in considering this bill, I find that the situation in Canada seems desperate; the government desires to upset and reorganize everything, it is intended to set aside provincial cooperative societies and other associations of farmers organized not only to improve farming methods but also to instruct farmers in the best methods to sell their products on the Canadian markets. All this is to be set aside and trade conditions in Canada are to be regulated.
First, the principle of the bill is wrong, it is wrong because it interferes with the practices and the privileges of the province of our Confederation. It is wrong because it invades the prerogatives of provincial governments which have organized their own methods of farming in connection with dairy products, cattle breeding and all things connected with agriculture and the dairy industry. Moreover, this bill sets up federal interference in private organizations. I contend that the government has no right to act thus, that this bill is ultra vires, nor has it the right-as the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Bury) has just stated- to tell the farmers: Your products do not belong to you, they are the property of every body. Since the effort was a personal one,
the farmers should have the right to trade as they please. In these times of modernism, when everywhere are to be found innovators whose ideas have absolutely nothing practical and who advocate principles which cannot be put into practice, the government delights in innovating everything with this bill which, if it were a declaration in a judicial case, it would be subject to as many motions for particulars as there are paragraphs.
I should not like to leave to my children a will thus drawn, because not one of the executors of any court of justice could understand it sufficiently to honestly apply the provisions affecting the various heirs.
Let us examine this bill. What is sought by it? What is the object? What is the Deus ex machina? I should like to meet the person who invented this scheme, the person who taught such principles to the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) and sought to create such privileges. Perchance are the tariff barriers of our country so high as to prevent our products being exported to the countries of Europe where they could be sold at a profit? Are the agreements of the Imperial Conference, held in Ottawa, not giving the results expected, is the sale of our Canadian products so small that our warehouses, to-day, are too full, and are we producing too much, because consumers have seen their purchasing power decrease?
Does the government wish, by means of this bill, to increase the price of our commodities or natural products? Then it would be a boom for the farmer. However, one must consider those who will purchase these products regulated by the Marketing Board and increase their purchasing power. This purchasing power is too restricted in this country, at present. We have not enough consumers, yet the government wishes to regulate exports and imports. I state that we will have to face a chaos in trade. Never will this be a success in this country, even if it be given a fair trial. This bill is simply a substitution to present to the farmers a sham Messiah just as the government presented to the unemployed in 1930. Some members were lucky enough to slide to Ottawa on butter. Today, the farmers are offered, with the idea of buttering them in the next election campaign, a new scheme which will disappear with the last ballot-box.

If we examine this bill, we find that it is divided into four parts. The first, is the minister-one that is not designated, a shadow minister. This bill seems one of the harbinger signs of the result of the inquiry on the spread of prices. Ploughing is done in a very abnormal way in the House of Commons. We are at the plough while awaiting the horses which are held up in committee. This time, so as to be practical and conform to their scheme of upsetting everything, our opponents have put the cart before the horses.
Will this shadow minister be the Minister of Agriculture or the Minister of Trade and Commerce? We do not know for he is not designated. Secondly, the Dominion Marketing Board; thirdly, the local board under the supervision of the dominion board; fourthly, the provincial marketing board. If these four working parts were put in a watch, I would feel sorry for the hands. It would never stop, the watch would never need winding. Section 3 of the bill reads as follows:

The governor in council may establish a board to be known as the Dominion Marketing Board to regulate the marketing of natural products as hereinafter provided.
But where are all our trade treaties? It strikes me that this is the home market, the local market of which we heard so much when we sat on your right, sir. However, this home market seems to have disappeared. The government intends to take possession of markets, create numerous channels, organize a commercial system, like a cartwheel, the nave of which will be the governor in council. No mention is made of the number of persons who will form part of this board; we do not know whence these people, these experts will come.
For some time past we have seen many experts in Canada, especially since 1930. For our banking affairs, the government sought an expert overseas in England. For our national ports inquiry the government also went overseas. There were no competent civil engineers in Canada. Where are we drifting to? There was another expert from overseas in connection with the last investigation. Briefly, there are no experts in Canada! Yet, there are men who have attained fame, highly gifted men, in this country, who could have been chairmen of these various commissions. Shall we again cross overseas to find a man having had experience with a marketing board so as to preside over the destinies of this Dominion Marketing Board? Paragraph 5 of section 3 reads as follows:
The board may, with the approval of the governor in council, employ such technical, professional and other officers and employees as the board may deem necessary or desirable, and such persons shall receive such salaries or remuneration as may be fixed by the board with the approval of the governor in council.
If we possess such men in this country, where are they? In the various departments? Why not allow Canada's commercial organization to remain as it is. Since confederation we have been putting into practice new and improved methods. Why destroy everything in 1934? Why renovate everything? I see no reason to set aside a long experience in trade, agriculture and mines so as to carry out innovations wtih this marketing bill which no one can understand; it is not clear and absolutely impractical.

I recall that the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell), who has had a large experience in agriculture, stated in this housS last year on two occasions that he was in favour of a marketing bill. Societies and associations of farmers and business men all over Canada have for many months, indeed years, been clamouring for just such a practical and beneficial measure as we have now before us, and now the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and his Quebec supporters are unearthing constitutional reasons for opposing it.
When I read the other day in Mr. Tasche-reau's organ, the Montreal Gazette, the interview in which he made such a violent attack on the federal government, I thought it was my duty to state my reasons for voting for this bill. I do not desire to be accused of misquoting him; therefore I shall give his statement as reported in the press:
"I do not know of a worse blow to Canadian unity and to the spirit that presided over confederation," declared Mr. Taschereau here last night in alluding to the federal government's marketing bill. . . .
"I note with much apprehension for the peace and well being of confederation, legislation now being discussed at Ottawa. I do not want it said' I am entering upon the federal domain; it is primarily the most vital interests of the provinces that are not only in jeopardy but in danger.
"First, the marketing bill. Ottawa wants to take control all at once of our forests, our mines, our fisheries, and our natural products. It will be easy enough to say ' no,' to this, but one sees the attempt being made and the spirit animating the dominion government."
Further on he says:
"I do not know of a worse blow to Canadian unity and to the spirit that presided over confederation. The danger is at our doors."
That is the amazing statement that Mr. Taschereau is reported to have proffered. Such sweeping allegations are too amazing to carry conviction to the minds of the people of Quebec. Mr. Taschereau has condemned himself by his own actions. When Bill No. 51 which we are now discussing was first introduced into this house, many provincial governments sent to the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) telegrams of approval and a great number of provincial legislatures then in session immediately passed unanimously the necessary enabling legislation in order that those provinces might cooperate with the federal government and their people enjoy the benefits of the marketing act. Mr. Taschereau himself, like the premiers of all the other provinces, received a copy of this bill, and what did he do? Did he denounce it in the Quebec house? Did he attempt then to show to the members of the Quebec assembly that this marketing board bill was detrimental to agriculture and industry and a blow to confederation? He merely expressed some doubts as to the propriety of the proposed legislation and immediately saw to it that the legislature unanimously pass a bill whereby the people of Quebec could cooperate with the federal government in the creation, operation and maintenance of a federal marketing board. The bill that was passed in the legislature of Quebec is bill No. 243, "an act to aid the putting into effect in this province of any federal act having as its object the marketing of the natural products of Canada and of any federal act respecting bankruptcy as regards compromises between creditors and debtors."
After Hon. Mr. Taschereau had taken such a commendable stand, he now turns round and in the most dramatic way asserts that confederation is threatened and the unity of Canada endangered by this bill. What logic! What consistency! If this bill were so bad, would it not have been the duty of the Quebec premier to refuse to pass the enabling legislation, which was nothing more or less than an approval of the federal measure? Nobody would have objected to Mr. Taschereau stating his reasons for refusing to commit his province to any policy which might destroy the so-called paramount rights of the province if such rights in his opinion were being encroached upon by the federal government. One might say that such views were highly hypercritical and were offered only for political reasons. However, I think the real motive for their utterance is the realization that the crisis is coming to an end, that unemployment is decreasing and, as the hon. member for East Edmonton (Mr. Bury) said a moment ago, prosperity is coming and is as inevitable as the rising of the sun above the horizon. The premier of Quebec

will then be deprived of the opportunity of making capital out of the depression and playing politics with the relief granted for unemployment, and he does not conceal his disappointment. On behalf of my native province I should like to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) for having initiated such a commendable piece of legislation at such an opportune time. As has been said by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Pickel), the prosperity of industry depends upon the prosperity of the farm. If you save the farm, you save the country; we are going to save the farm and thereby save the country. I need not repeat what has been so clearly stated by my hon. friends on this side, that the purpose of this bill is to provide for the orderly marketing of farm produce in order to stop competition between producers, regularize production, improve the quality of farm products, regulate

exports and arrange and promote cooperation between producers so that they may be assured of a reasonable profit. The agricultural marketing bill introduced in the House of Commons by Hon. Robert Weir,

The new federal marketing act, officially known as the Natural Products Marketing Act, is now before parliament. It is a farreaehing measure, drastic in some of its clauses, radical in thought, but a piece of legislation that comes into being because of absolute necessity. The act is destined to help those industries which, apparently, cannot help themselves. It provides for the appointment of a federal marketing board to supervise, control and organize trade, to give some guidance and direction to producers, in order that production plans may harmonize with market requirements and to prevent, as far as possible, undue fluctuations in supply, should prove to be a step forward'. Indeed, the useful results of planned marketing, once the necessary unity of policy has been obtained, are so evident as to warrant measures being taken to bring this about. Thus we find legislation to this end in Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, the United Kingdom and the United States. In all the principle is practically the same, that is, to make possible the control of the entire distribution of any product, or in any one area, and so prevent the ruinous so-called competition which, instead of being the life of trade, has proven to be the death of business. He has been a detriment to those

Mr. Speaker, it is with a degree of reluctance, a reluctance due in part only to some physical disability, that I rise at this stage of the proceedings to take part in the discussion upon the measure now before the house. I am impelled to do so by two main considerations: the importance of the measure itself as it may and as it undoubtedly will affect the great body of producers in Canada and the great percentage of the people of my riding and my province, and the fact that I have been among those who have consistently urged the introduction of legislation of this kind. My first words, therefore, must be of congratulation to the government and more particularly to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) upon the courage and initiative shown in bringing forward a measure of this type; to use the words of the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston), the courage to take new paths, to open up new roads and to move forward in a new direction when times demand and when circumstances make it essential; and also upon their appreciation not only of the conditions which exist but of the responsibility of the state in respect of those problems.

Marketing Act-Mr. Speakman
It is not my purpose, nor does it conform, as I understand the matter, with the position which I occupy in the house, that I should snter into a detailed defence of this measure; that is the duty of the government which gave this legislation birth and of the party under whose auspices it was brought forth. Nor is it my place to enter upon a lengthy counter attack upon those who do not view this matter as I do. I was not elected to this house as a political partisan, and during the thirteen years I have sat in this chamber it has been my effort to cooperate with either or both parties in regard to any meritorious legislation which might be introduced. That stand I propose to maintain at this time. I shall therefore confine myself in the main to stating my views upon this proposed legislation and its possible effects, and to indicate why I welcome and shall support this measure on second reading. In doing so I shall endeavour to discuss the matter very briefly under three main heads: the conditions in this country and the world which make such legislation necessary and essential; the objectives which should be achieved if we are to meet and remedy those conditions, and the extent to which, in my opinion, this bill will meet these essentials and will accomplish these objectives.
As to the conditions themselves, Mr. Speaker, they are matters quite understood and appreciated by every hon. member of this house whose occupation, location or duties bring him into contact with the main bodies of our producers of natural products, and particularly our farmers. The conditions are obvious; that cannot be gainsaid: The condition under which we have violent fluctuations in the prices of farm products, fluctuations either arbitrary or fortuitous but equally calamitous in their effects; the conditions under which we have spreads which we believe to be unnecessary and far too great between the price received by the producer and the price paid by the consumer and the condition, above all, under which year after year the farmers of this country-certainly I can speak for western Canada, and I think for all Canada in that respect-receive less for their products than will enable them to maintain a decent standard of living and meet their obligations. Nor are the effects of those conditions confined to the producers themselves. We have had discussed in this house time and again the condition of the provinces, and particularly of the western provinces, and criticism has been made because loans and

guarantees have been given in order to assist their finances. Why are the western provinces in that situation? Speaking now particularly for the three prairie provinces, where the great majority of the population are farmers, I can say that the financial situation of these provinces is not due to inherent defects in government or to extravagance in expenditure. I know that in my own province, and I believe in the other provinces, expenditures have been cut to the bone. No, the trouble goes deeper; the roots are in the ground, and the fact is that the majority of the taxpayers of these provinces are farmers. When the majority of the taxpayers are not receiving sufficient income to enable them to buy the necessities of life, let alone pay their taxes, government finances must suffer. There are only two sources open to any provincial government from which they may obtain revenue, namely taxation or borrowing; when the taxpayer fails borrowing is the last resort. But borrowing brings with it its own punishment and its own destruction in the accumulation of interest charges which result. There, Mr. Speaker, is a phase which vitally affects every taxpayer and every citizen in Canada. I think this should be taken into full consideration when the bill is being discussed, for only by an appreciation of these facts can we understand the measure now before us.
Then, leaving the domestic situation, we look to the world about us and what do we find? The situation has wholly changed within the last two decades. The time was, and not so very long ago, when apart from tariff restrictions in the various importing countries, the goods of all countries could be sold on a competitive basis; to the best man or the lowest price went the market. That was the day of freedom of sale, so called; that was the day of individual competition. But, Mr. Speaker, that day has gone and in its place we have not only tariff restriction but the exclusion of certain commodities; we have commodities admitted only under quota restriction as to quantity, as to quality, as to the percentage of goods from our country which may be used in proportion to similar goods of domestic origin. We may regret this situation; we may look upon it as detrimental, but facts are stubborn things. With other members of the house I have indulged in certain theories, but I have found that when a theory comes in conflict with an established fact it is usually the theory that is shattered and the fact that remains. This is something that must be taken into consider-

ation, and in view of these facts legislation of some form to meet the existing conditions becomes not only necessary but essential.
Now I should like to say a word as to the definite objects which must be accomplished if these conditions are to be met. I am firmly convinced of the merits of cooperation in meeting problems of this kind. By that I mean cooperation among the producers themselves and the elimination, by mutual consent, of the self destructive and mutually destructive competition which prevails as between individuals. I believe that only by the encouragement, the assistance and the development of true cooperation, with all that it implies such as the increased intelligence of the producer, the increased self help of the producer and the working together of the producers, can the matter be solved. But we find another condition. I am not speaking now of wheat, which is a problem by itself; I am speaking of almost every other product of the farm from fruit to eggs. You will find that from ninety-five to ninety-eight per cent of the total production of each of those products is consumed within this country and that we export five per cent or less of each. Yet it has been borne out not only by our experience but by the statements of those in the trade that this small, insignificant export has shattered and brought to chaos the domestic price year after year, season after season. And again, any proposed measure which does not contain within itself the power to deal with such a situation must fail, for the domestic cooperation between producers cannot take care of the situation.
These are the main points which I believe must be covered, and I would emphasize particularly the necessity of securing to the producer a greater proportion of the price paid by the consumer. More than that, we must try to secure to the producer a return which will enable him to continue his operations, meet his liabilities and pay his taxes, and will restore to him that buying power the lack of which has been one of the chief causes of the depression which has fallen so heavily upon us and upon other countries as well. These are some of the things which must be accomplished, Mr. Speaker, and now I turn to this bill to see to what degree and in what measure the objectives desired may be achieved by it.
Before I do that, however, may I offer this suggestion: I have said that I am a believer in cooperation, and that argument has been advanced by many of those who oppose this bill. To my mind the present measure is rooted and founded in cooperation, for how 74726-164
otherwise can it succeed? It demands, and to a large degree has already received through enabling legislation, the cooperation of the provinces. It demands for its success, and indeed for its very life, the cooperation of the producers themselves. May I say again- because this is essentially important-that the very genius of this bill, the very basis and spirit of this legislation, is the cooperation which will be received by this federal body from those who will be more directly interested, and from the provinces who are in close touch with the problems of their own citizens.
I come now to the bill, and what do we find there? The bill proposes to set up a federal board which, acting as the general director of the bill and of the marketing plans, shall work in cooperation with and in conjunction with boards appointed by the provinces, each in their own sphere, and each to deal with matters which come under their jurisdiction. Further, the board is to work in cooperation with the local boards, which, as I understand it, will be appointed largely by the producers who will be beneficially affected. That is the scope of the bill. To that board and to the boards which will cooperate with it are given ample, wide powers -possibly too wide, but I do not think so. For we are meeting a condition the ramifications of which are as yet barely understood, and to my mind nothing could be more fatal than to hamper and restrict the board in respect of its statutory powers before it commenced operations, so that when it did meet with preblems it would not be able to deal with them promptly.
It has been suggested that parliament itself should deal with them. To my mind parliament is the last body in the world which could deal with the emergent situations as they arise. All parliament can do and all parliament should do is to pass such legislation and to delegate such powers, so that under the authority of those powers the executive may deal with each situation day by day, taking into consideration the individual merits of each case as occasion may arise. The powers, then, are wide.
Then, among the powers what do we find? We find the power to register, if necessary, the names and the addresses of the producers. And what of it? The very members in this house who criticize on that ground were most urgent that a given or stipulated percentage of the producers in each branch or of each product should indicate their approval, or by petition indicate their desire, that some scheme or plan should be put into force.

How could that be accomplished? How could parliament or the governor in council or the board have the slightest idea what percentage of voices had spoken or how many of the people were interested unless beforehand they knew how many had a right to speak? Then, the bill speaks of licensing. I doubt whether the government knows, and I am quite certain the house does not know, to what extent this licensing may have to be applied. However, the fact is that the power is given to license-and to license what? The clause which applies to licensing includes producers and dealers in the products. It is quite conceivable to me that anybody dealing in those products should be licensed. The power is there. Further, it gives to the board the power of restriction and control of exports. And, Mr. Speaker, how could that situation which I have described and which is familiar to all of us be met in any other way?-that situation under which a comparatively small export, an infinitesimal percentage of the production, is allowed to destroy and crush the price of the entire domestic product. How else could it be done? We have had some experience along those lines. Within the last three years a cooperative organization in Canada entered into a mutually satisfactory and mutually profitable arrangement with the great consumers' cooperative of Great Britain. On the one hand we had the Canadian cooperative live stock shippers and on the other the British consumers. It was an ideal arrangement-the hungry mouths at one end and the eager sellers at the other. On what rock did they split? They split upon the rock which has destroyed and made impossible the profitable shipment of live stock, hog products and various other products during the past number of years. Because of the fact that during certain seasons of the year the price offered for cattle and other products in Great Britain is higher than the price in Canada, exporters rushed to export their products, thereby creating a surplus upon the market. Then comes the season when perhaps Irish cattle may come on the market-this may not happen to-day but did at one time-and as a result the price falls

below the level of that obtaining in Canada with the result that export ceases. The stipulation made by the British authority was this: "We are willing to receive your live stock, but we insist upon having continuity of supply week by week, month by month, season by season throughout the twelve months of the year." That was the condition. Now, hon. members cannot expect any single exporter to export at a loss, nor should we be right in expecting any such thing. Under this bill power is given not only to hold back and restrict during a time when an over supply might destroy the market abroad and break the price, but also to send forward during the slack months, at times when goods may be sold at a loss, the necessary quantity to relieve the domestic market, thereby destroying the surplus, and to reimburse the exporters or producers who under such conditions and circumstances send forth that surplus. Thus will assistance be given to all producers in Canada. That is only right and wise.
In what other way could we meet a situation such as I have described, such as other hon. members have described and which hon. members know exists, under which importers in the country purchasing our goods are restricted by quotas, and restricted as to quality, quantity, time and kind? Only by some central guiding body with power to act can that situation and can the conditions imposed upon us, conditions for which no government in Canada has been responsible, over which we have no control and with which we must comply, be met.
Then, too there is the control of imports. I shall not refer, save in passing, to the exaggerated arguments advanced in this respect by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). References have been made to the incongruity of the arguments of the right hon. gentleman. The bill provides that natural products of other countries which may come into competition with regulated natural products of Canada, may be kept out or restricted as to quantity. Under that provision it is suggested that oranges and coffee may be kept out of the country. It is news to me, Mr. Speaker, to learn that either oranges or coffee are natural products of Canada, or come into direct competition with regulated products grown in Canada. These are bugbears, and to my mind the very extravagance of the argument is one of the arguments in favour of the bill, because it shows how far afield people may sometimes go to find substantial arguments to justify their position.

Those are the main essentials of the bill, as I see them. I have read it from beginning to end, clause after clause, and nowhere do I find a power given to the board or to subsidiary boards to control, to check or to limit production. And, Mr. Speaker, that is one thing our farmers from one end of Canada to the other are demanding, namely that this lack of control which has brought them into the chaotic situation in which they now find themselves, with resulting loss to Canada, the closing down of our factories, and unemployment among our labouring classes, due to the lack of purchasing power of the farmer, shall cease. They demand that this uncontrolled situation shall be taken in hand, and shall be taken in hand by the one body in Canada competent to deal with it, namely the federal government. May I say further that the pictures that have been drawn of what might come to pass under this board apparently presuppose and are based upon one idea, namely that any board appointed would deem it to be its duty, its main objective, its ideal, to hamper and restrict and destroy the very producers for whose benefit the board is being brought into existence. I am taking it for granted that this government, and a Liberal government if again it should get into power, would have enough common sense, enough regard for their own political safety and appreciation of their own responsibility, at least to see that the best possible results be achieved. I am taking for granted, and I am confident, that if by some strange chance or by some diabolical interposition a board should come into existence that had for its objective the destruction of the interests it is intended to serve, the tearing down instead of building up, the provincial boards 74726-164^
would refuse to cooperate; the board appointed under the act would cease to function, and the act would be null and void.
For these reasons I shall not only support the bill on its second reading but, as I have said, I welcome its introduction. My criticism, if criticism I should offer at this time and which should more appropriately come during the committee stage, would be not that the powers given to the board are not limited, but that the bill itself embraces too much.
To my mind the problem of marketing the farm products of this country apart from wheat, because of the importance of the great diversity of products embraced in the general term "mixed farming" would provide a problem sufficient to engage the attention and occupy the time and utilize all the genius of any board which could possibly be appointed.
Personally I should not like to see wheat included in this bill, for the very simple reason that the problem of the disposition of our wheat is one wholly different and apart from the problem confronting our mixed farmers. What is the problem of the wheat farmer? It is the problem of the disposal of a great export crop, a worldwide product, graded, standardized. It is a problem of selling the great bulk of that product in export markets. The domestic market for wheat, while important, is relatively insignificant. The problem lies in the export market, in meeting the agreements which have been entered into and the quotas which have been put into effect. But apart from that the business itself is sufficiently great, of sufficient importance and sufficiently onerous, to occupy the full time and attention of a properly constituted wheat board, and I hope that at some time in the not too distant future this bill will be supplemented by another creating a federal wheat board to do for wheat what I hope this bill will do for mixed farming products.
I cannot speak of the products of the forest, for frankly, I cannot understand that reference in the bill. The products of the forest in their natural condition, as I understand it, are logs. When are logs manufactured? Is lumber a manufactured article? If it is, then it does not come within the scope of this bill, because it is certainly neither food nor drink. It would be classed perhaps with furniture and boots and shoes.
Speaking of boots and shoes, if I may digress for a moment, when the hon. member for East Edmonton (Mr. Bury) was making his eloquent and occasionally humourous address, he placed a certain interpretation

Marketing Act-Mr. Speakman
on the reference made to boots and shoes by the leader of the opposition. I have in mind another interpretation, another idea concerning the matter. I wonder if boots and shoes come in from the fact that on this bill, at least, occasionally when he opened his mouth he put his foot in it. But is lumber a manufactured article? Paper certainly is; articles of pulp certainly must be, and to what extent would this bill apply? I do not know and frankly am not keenly interested or well informed on the subject; there are those who know much more about it than I do. But while I may deprecate the inclusion within the scope of the bill of certain matters which I believe are extraneous and should be kept out, I am certainly not going to cut off my own nose to spite my face or vote against a bill which I believe will benefit the farmers simply because it may benefit others also. To my mind that would be a rather narrow view to take of my duties in this house.
In conclusion may I make one reference to a remark that was made by a speaker this afternoon. The hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst), in the very fine address which he gave to the house, spoke of the world marching on and of the necessity of the country and parliament marching on with it or being left behind in a hopeless bog. The thought came into my mind that if we are going to march on we have two alternatives: we may march on with the world in its progress as a disorderly, unorganized mob of selfdestructive individuals, and if so we march to certain defeat and individual extinction; or we may march on with the world as a disciplined mutually supporting body of troops to take part in that glorious world victory over penury and want which I hope will be achieved ere long. My convictions lie with the self disciplined army, not with the disorganized mob of individuals. This is a measure through which a number at least of our people may organize and discipline themselves and take a world part in that forward march.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, and others which may be developed during the committee stage when the details of the bill may properly be discussed, I welcome and support this legislation.
Mr. JOSEPH THAUYETTE (Vaudreuil-
Soulanges) (Translation): Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to delay the house very long in debating the bill under consideration. I followed closely and with much interest the various speeches delivered by hon. members this afternoon and this evening; I was very much impressed with the various views set forth.

One speech especially interested me. Each time the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon) speaks in the house, I listen with interest because I look upon him as a brilliant orator, a legal light. I have noticed that each time he takes part in a debate, or at least often, he specially criticizes the government of his province. He quite strongly attacked, this evening, the Quebec premier, the Hon. Mr. Taschereau, and gave proof that he had special aptitudes as an official critic. I think, sir, that the hon. member as well as his friends must greatly regret that he was not chosen as leader of the opposition for Quebec, at the convention held in Sherbrooke last year. He would have been more at home and the charges he has made against the Quebec government would have produced more effect, had he made them as the official leader of the opposition, face to face with the Quebec premier. I trust that the people of his party will recognize this fact at the next election.
After closely reading Bill No. 51, now under consideration by the house, I deem it my duty, as representative of a county where farming is the main industry, if not the only one, to express my humble views on the timeliness of such an act. At this stage of the discussion one must consider the principle on which the government based itself to bring down such a measure. To what authority does the government intend to entrust the enforcement of this act? What powers will be granted to this authority to administer this act throughout the country? How will the regulations, orders and decisions issued by the central board at Ottawa, be promulgated throughout the various provinces? How will these orders be transmitted? There are many questions which it would be rational to inquire into before adopting the bill and enforcing it.
Will the benefits, which it is hoped to obtain for the producers in the application of this act, be in proportion to the losses which might be incurred through the working of this so intricate mechanism of associations, councils or boards transmitting their decisions from place to place so as to finally reach the central board or vice versa, in connection with the marketing or exportation of the products regulated by this organization?
Throughout the whole range of this hierarchy of officials, will there not be discrimination as against a certain class of citizen who will be cared for only after these large associations have taken the best of the market? Will intelligent men, experts in their trade or profession, with a long experience, comply with the regulations of these local or provin-

Marketing Act-Mr. Thauvette
cial boards which, from their viewpoint at least, have never been associated with the profession or trade to which they belong?
I intend, sir, to reply to these questions by the various sections embodied in this bill.
First, if I restrict myself to the reading of the preamble of this bill, I find nothing which would warrant us to have any fear:
An act to improve the methods and practices of marketing of natural products in Canada and in export trade, and to make further provision in connection therewith.
No danger lies behind this title. It reminds one of the chocolate coating under which the druggist conceals his drugs to render them tasteless. If we had only to deal with the preamble, truly I would have no objection to approve of this bill. Seeing that for the last four years I have requested the government on various occasions, to help the farmer by finding him markets and obtaining better prices for the sale of his products; I regret to note, however, that ever since this government is at the helm of affairs in this country, it has done nothing to help the most numerous and important class of our population, the farming class.
In examining this bill, we find, under interpretation, the word "minister" and the definition for the requirements of this act:
"Minister means the minister designated by the governor in council to administer this act."
This, sir, is another snag added to our constitution.
By this act it is intended to suppress parliamentary rights, withdraw from the representatives of the people the right of legislating on the various questions which concern citizens, their financial, professional or trade interests, so as to confer upon a board or boards whose members are unknown and have not yet been chosen, the power of making regulations.

Do you
contend that it is legal?

The minister is granted-is it the Minister of Agriculture or the Minister of Trade and Commerce? The act makes no mention'-the power to legislate. At all events, the whole mechanism of this bureaucratic machinery will be put into motion by the promulgation of an order in council. The government's policy of governing by orders in council still continues. Governing behind closed doors. The government has made it a principle to disregard the people's wishes and assumes the rights and privileges which parliament possesses of legislating in the interest of the nation on such
vital questions as those at present involved. After the renewal of the signature in blank, the government intends to regulate the natural resources which belong to the provinces, such as forests, mines, fisheries, etc. That is the attitude which the government has taken ever since I have the honour of being a member of this house. We have had these last years a dictatorship which resembles that of Mussolini. We were heading for Moscow; now we have been switched on the road to Berlin.
May I, sir, discuss a few points of this bill. In examining the various sections which will determine the enforcement and working of the act submitted to us, we find at section 3, paragraph 6:
The board shall be a body corporate and shall have power for the purposes of this act to acquire, hold and dispose of real and personal property.
I am amazed at the powers conferred on this board-which will legally be constituted by the governor in council-to hold, acquire and dispose of real and personal property, not under the authority of parliament but by order in council. Such properties are to be acquired, not under the authority of parliament but by order in council, they are to be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund. If I understand the wording of the act, they will belong to the board which acquired them and may be disposed of as they think fit and for its own use.
Section 3, paragraph 9 reads as follows:
The governor in council may from time to time authorize payment to the board, out of the consolidated revenue fund, of such sums of money as may be necessary for the purpose of this act.
Always by order in council, the minister may draw from the treasury the sums of money it pleases, turn them over to the board which will pay the amounts deemed necessary for the purposes of this act. Certainly this provision will provide for the expenditure of sums of money drawn from the treasury, without parliament being given an opportunity to discuss whether they are necessary or even being given the opportunity of investigating matters.
However, sir, what seems to me most arbitrary and at the same time most annoying to the farmers of this country who will have to carry on their marketing every day by virtue of the act, are the powers defined in section 4 of the bill, subsection 1, paragraph (a):
(a) to regulate the time and place of marketing the regulated product, and to determine the manner of distribution and the quantity and quality or grade of the regulated

Marketing Act-Mr. Thauvette
product that shall be marketed by any person at any time, and to prohibit the marketing of any of the regulated product of any grade or quality;
Can. one realize what confusion will be created among producers by putting into force this provision of the act! Can one imagine the recriminations and protests which will be forthcoming from all sides when all and each of these small producers will have to sell or ship all or part of their products to the market! I do not intend to question all the farmers of my constituency so as .to find out their views; however, a large number have already protested. This section to my mind nationalizes the commerce of our natural products. It is state monopoly of personal liberty. It paralyzes all private enteprises. It smothers all personal ambition since the output of each and every producer can be restricted.
Are we assured that the preference shown by some farmers to produce certain products instead of others will be respected. Is the board going to meddle with the affairs of every one, annoy these good farmers so as to verify their licences or compel them to join associations which they will very little appreciate? This is one of the provisions to which I have strong objections. The people of this country are not prepared for socialism, they will not easily sacrifice their commercial liberties. Why this state management or rather this nationalization of the commerce of natural products, and why not act likewise with manufactured products?
Is it thought that the government's high tariff have sufficiently protected the manufacturers? Yet reports come in every day from the tariff board informing us that a large number of manufacturers of various goods protest against the high tariffs. They request lower tariffs so as to increase their trade.
I contend, sir, that the same thing will happen with natural products if the government enforces this regulated production and marketing of natural products by order in council.
This will have the effect of creating an atmosphere of uncertainty on the markets where it is hoped to sell the products, an uncertainty as to prices and quantity. The reaction might well prove to be a decrease in the sales. Does any one think that the farmer can keep in storage for an indefinite time perishable goods? All are aware that those who take up breeding for market purposes cannot keep these young herds, which are ready for the market, for an indefinite time. And how many such instances are there! I can well imagine the reception awaiting these

gentlemen of the board when they appear on the market to prohibit the sale of the farmer's herds. The government will be apprised sooner than it expects of the protests coming from the four corners of this country.
This legislation is the result of the high tariff policy advocated by this government and clearly intended to win over the support of those who sit on the extreme left. We have witnessed these last days our friends on the extreme left embrace in a fatherly way this new bom Tory infant as if it were their legitimate child. We have again noted that extremes meet and often have some affinity; however, I wish to point out that the truth is to be found in the golden mean.
Therefore, I would approve a bill introduced by this government purporting to help the farmers in improving the quality of their products. I would gladly support a bill which would be a scheme to help the farmers in their present organizations, farmers' unions, cooperative societies, etc., so as to make these associations more efficient and powerful, in order that their members could obtain a more abundant return and make larger profits on their production.
I cannot be convinced, sir, that producers would be benefited by restricting production. Moreover, would it be human, in these times, to restrict the production of the prime necessities of life, when we are aware that there are so many people that suffer for the lack of the necessary things of life while others have none!
If the government wants to show its good intentions towards the Canadian producers, especially the farmers, let it put at their disposal all the means capable of benefiting them by legislating in a constitutional way, by introducing a bill which would benefit those interested inasmuch as it would be applicable through conviction rather than through constraint.
In closing my remarks, sir, I wish to express my views on section 14 of this bill.
Offences
14. Every person who fails to comply with any order or determination of the board or of a local board or any regulation of the governor in council shall be guilty of an offence and punishable on summary conviction with a fine of not less than twenty-five dollars and not more than five hundred dollars, or to imprisonment not exceeding three months, or to both fine and imprisonment.
I loathe to think that this section will render a great service to Canadian producers. Will parliament be held responsible for the

C.N.R.-Finance
enforcement of this section in connection with offences against any order or determination of the board or governor in council? Does the government always intend to carry on by blasting? This policy has already failed. I do not think it will be a success this time. That is why I cannot approve of this bill.
